title: Is the PSM Worth It in 2026? (Honest Verdict)
dek: Yes, for almost anyone targeting agile or Scrum roles: the PSM I is affordable, respected, never expires, and you can self-study it. No, if your target jobs are traditional, plan-driven project management — a PMI credential fits better.

seo.metaTitle: Is the PSM Certification Worth It? (2026)
seo.metaDescription: An honest 2026 verdict on the PSM (Professional Scrum Master) — real cost, why it never expires, who genuinely benefits, and who should skip it.

sources.label: Scrum.org — Professional Scrum Master I (PSM I) certification

body.richText: The Professional Scrum Master (PSM I), from Scrum.org, is one of the best-value certifications in the whole project management field. But "good value" isn't the same as "right for you." Here's the honest verdict, including who should skip it.

The short answer: worth it for almost anyone aiming at agile or Scrum roles — it's cheap, respected, and never expires. Not worth it if your target work is traditional, plan-driven project management, where a PMI credential carries more weight.

body.text: What it is and what it costs

body.richText: The PSM I certifies that you understand the Scrum framework and how to apply it. Unlike many certifications, it has three unusually friendly traits: the exam voucher costs about $200, no training course is required (you can self-study), and — crucially — it never expires and has no renewal fee. Pay once, keep it for life.

items: Excellent value — a respected credential for around $200, with no course to buy
It never expires and has no renewal cost, unlike most certifications
Its demanding 85% pass mark makes it a credible signal of real understanding
No prerequisites — accessible to career-changers and beginners
Directly relevant to the agile and software roles where Scrum is the norm
It's knowledge-based — passing proves you understand Scrum, not that you've run it
For traditional, waterfall-heavy industries, a PMI credential is more recognized
The market has many certified Scrum Masters, so it won't make you unique on its own
Employer-sponsored learners may prefer the course-based CSM (someone else pays)

body.richText: Who it's NOT for: people targeting traditional project management roles (get a PMI credential instead), and anyone expecting a certificate alone to land the job. The PSM proves knowledge — you still need to demonstrate facilitation experience in interviews.

richText: The other big Scrum Master certification is the CSM from the Scrum Alliance, which requires a paid two-day course. If you're self-funding, the PSM I is usually the better value; if your employer is paying for a guided course, the CSM is fine. We compare them in detail in

items.question: Is the PSM I worth it for beginners?
items.answerRichText: Yes. It has no prerequisites, no required course, and never expires, so it's an accessible and low-risk first credential for anyone targeting agile roles. Its tough 85% pass mark also makes it a credible signal.

items.question: Does the PSM certification expire?
items.answerRichText: No. Unlike most certifications, the PSM I never expires and has no renewal fee — you pay the exam once and keep the credential for life.
